# Future of Families: Cardiovascular Health Among Young Adults Cohort Study: Rationale, Key Questions, Study Design, and Participant Characteristics

**Authors:** Donald M Lloyd‐Jones; Norrina B Allen; James Stein; Hongyan Ning; Kristin Hansen; Lifang Hou; Nicole J Katchur; Claudia Korcarz; Iulia Kotenko; Shantelle Little; Colter Mitchell; Jessica Rooney; Hacer Savas; Lisa Schneper; Elisabeth Tawa; Linda Van Horn; Yinan Zheng; Russell Tracy; Noreen Goldman; Daniel A Notterman

**Affiliations:** 1 Framingham Center for Population & Prevention Research and Section of Preventive Medicine & Epidemiology, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, MA, USA | 2 Department of Preventive Medicine, Northwestern Feinberg School of Medicine, Chicago, IL, USA | 3 Atherosclerosis Imaging Research Program, University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health, Madison, WI, USA | 4 Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA | 5 Population Studies Center, Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA | 6 Department of Pathology & Lab Medicine, and Biochemistry, Larner College of Medicine, University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA | 7 Office of Population Research and School of Public and International Affairs, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA

## Abstract

Childhood social determinants of adult cardiovascular health and potential mechanisms that link them are poorly understood. The FF‐CHAYA (Future of Families–Cardiovascular Health Among Young Adults) study is designed to address these knowledge gaps.

The FF‐CHAYA sample is a subcohort of the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study, which enrolled 4897 mother–baby dyads at delivery beginning in 1998 to 2000 and collected extensive data on neighborhood, family, school, and behavioral exposures at birth and offspring ages 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, and 22 years. From 2021 to 2023, we performed an in‐person examination on 1421 offspring, including obtaining questionnaire responses addressing health status and health behaviors, and performance of anthropometry, blood pressure measurement, phlebotomy, and carotid ultrasonography using standardized protocols. An additional 620 offspring answered questionnaires electronically. Cardiovascular health status was quantified using the Life's Essential 8 score (0–100; higher is better cardiovascular health). Measurement of carotid intima‐media thickness, grayscale lucency, and carotid distensibility was performed.

Among 1975 nonpregnant participants, mean age was 23.2±0.8 years, 55% identified as female, 19.5% White, 49.1% Black, 26.7% Hispanic, and 4.7% as Asian or multiple race/ethnicity. Mean body mass index was 29.0±8.2 kg/m2, and mean Life's Essential 8 score was 69.2±13.0 points, with significant variation by demographic groups. Carotid measures indicate accelerated early arterial injury.

This article describes the rationale, study design and methods, and characteristics of the FF‐CHAYA cohort, a novel longitudinal study designed to examine associations of childhood social determinants with young adult cardiovascular health and early arterial injury, as well as potential epigenetic mechanisms that may mediate these associations.

Keywords: cardiovascular health, carotid ultrasound, epigenetics, social determinants

## What Is New?

- This article describes the rationale, key questions, methods, and baseline characteristics of a novel cohort of young adults (mean age 23.2 years) from disadvantaged social backgrounds, followed longitudinally since birth with serial measurements of social determinants of health (SDoH).

- Cardiovascular health status, measured by the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 score, was suboptimal, and measures of carotid imaging suggested advanced early arterial injury in these young adults.

## What Question Should Be Addressed Next?

- Ongoing studies are examining associations of early‐life social determinants of health with young adult cardiovascular health and arterial injury, and potential molecular mechanisms mediating these associations; the investigators welcome collaboration.

## INTRODUCTION

This article describes the rationale, key questions, study design, methods, and baseline characteristics of the study participants of the FF‐CHAYA (Future of Families–Cardiovascular Health Among Young Adults) Study. FF‐CHAYA is a novel longitudinal cohort study designed to examine associations of social determinants of health (SDoH) measured throughout childhood with young adult cardiovascular health (CVH) and early arterial injury. We observed suboptimal levels of CVH, notably high mean body mass index (BMI) levels, and evidence of early arterial injury in this cohort of young adults with disadvantaged social circumstances since birth. Future work will examine correlates of these findings and potential epigenetic and other mechanisms that may mediate these associations.

### Rationale for the Study

Cardiovascular disease (CVD; including atherosclerotic CVD, heart failure, and stroke) remains the leading cause of death and disability for adults in the United States and worldwide. 1 Recent projections from the American Heart Association suggest that, by 2050, more than 45 million American adults will have clinical CVD and more than 184 million (>61%) will have clinical CVD or hypertension, its most prevalent underlying risk factor. 2 As a result, inflation‐adjusted direct health care costs related to CVD risk factors are projected to triple between 2020 and 2050, to $1.34 trillion annually, and direct costs related to clinical CVD conditions are projected to rise from $393 billion to $1.49 trillion. 3

The burden of CVD and its determinants, however, is not distributed evenly in the population. CVD and its risk factors disproportionately affect underrepresented racial and ethnic groups and those of lower socioeconomic status, and these disparities are projected to widen, particularly for groups who identify as Black, Hispanic, multiracial, or American Indian/Alaska Native. 1 , 2 Increasing obesity prevalence in children is of particular concern, given its central role in driving incidence of other causal CVD risk factors in adolescence and young adulthood, leading to earlier and higher cumulative exposures to CVD risk factors and resulting vascular and cardiac damage. 4 , 5 Indeed, exposures to all of the traditional CVD risk factors, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, and smoking in childhood drive adult subclinical disease and clinical events. 6 , 7 Thus, early‐life determinants of CVH behaviors and health factors are of particular interest, because they may drive lifelong CVH trajectories (adversely or positively).

In recent years, SDoH have received significant attention as upstream societal and structural factors that drive the propensity for beneficial or adverse health outcomes. The World Health Organization defines SDoH as the “structural determinants and conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age” that affect health, functioning, and quality of life. 8 There are 5 key domains of SDoH: economic stability, neighborhood and built environment, education, social and community context, and health and health care. 9 These constructs cover a number of critical factors including socioeconomic status, adverse life course experiences, social support, family structure, access to care, neighborhood environment, and stress, including stress associated with perceived or actual discrimination. 10 , 11 Data on SDoH among middle‐aged adults are increasingly available, as are longitudinal associations with downstream health outcomes. However, investigations examining the full array of SDoH in children and prospective associations with health outcomes are rare. Existing studies are often limited by retrospective data collection on SDoH, introducing the potential for significant recall bias and imprecision of exposure measurements. Thus, the true nature and magnitude of longitudinal associations of SDoH during early life, a critical period of exposure, with young adult health outcomes are largely unknown.

Whereas studies have linked socioeconomic status in childhood with adult risk factors and CVD events, 12 , 13 , 14 data are sparse on the broad array of SDoH in contemporary samples of children, in whom decreasing CVH and the onset of CVD appear to be occurring relatively earlier in life than in prior generations. 15 , 16 , 17 The pervasive influence of socioeconomic disparities, environmental stressors, and limited access to preventive health care may further accelerate the deterioration of CVH in youth, underscoring the need for timely and comprehensive interventions targeting SDoH in children. A recent meta‐analysis found that almost all studies showed a relationship between childhood adversity and adult CVD risk. 18 Indeed, there is an emerging consensus that the origins of adult disease, including CVD, are in part developmental, reflecting adverse maternal, uterine, and early‐life physical and social environments. Epigenetic modification, such as DNA methylation, may be a central mechanism through which environmental and behavioral exposures can “get under the skin” and influence phenotypes and health outcomes at the molecular level. 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 Another mechanism may be through alterations in the gut microbiome. 27 , 28 , 29

Advances in noninvasive imaging of arteries in living individuals have provided direct visualization of arterial injury and atherosclerosis progression, which begins in the first and second decades of life and proceeds across the life course. One of the most feasible, sensitive, and reliable ways of imaging subclinical arterial injury in adolescents and young adults uses B‐mode carotid artery (CA) ultrasound to measure intima‐media thickness (IMT), an indicator of arterial injury, and distensibility, a sensitive measure of arterial stiffening. Numerous studies have examined carotid IMT measures, and their antecedent risk factors, in children and adults. 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 A number of recent studies have linked both childhood SDoH and CVH metrics with later carotid measures. 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 , 42 In turn, carotid IMT measured in adulthood is consistently associated with future clinical CVD events, including both myocardial infarction and stroke, and mortality. 43 , 44 However, data are lacking regarding associations of early‐life SDoH and epigenetic measures with young adult carotid IMT and CA distensibility. More novel image analysis techniques can also characterize grayscale echogenicity and texture of the arterial wall, indicating early arterial injury. Grayscale measures can predict future CVD events in asymptomatic individuals, independent of carotid IMT, 45 , 46 and alterations in these grayscale measures are associated with obesity, inflammatory biomarkers, T‐cell subpopulations, and their changes over time, providing insights into development of subclinical vascular disease.

To better delineate the prospective associations between early‐life SDoH and young adult CVH and subclinical CVD, we leveraged an existing large social science study, the FFCWS (Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study), 47 that began in 1998 to 2000. FFCWS is the longest‐running and only contemporary prospective birth cohort study of young adults in the United States, based on a national sample. FFCWS has unique strengths in the depth and repeated measures of social phenotyping across the entirety of early life, making it an ideal venue for the present study. 47 , 48 From September 2021 through December 2023, we conducted an innovative in‐person cohort examination, measuring CVH metrics and indicators of early vascular damage among young adult offspring participants (mean age 23 years) who have been followed since birth with frequent, in‐depth phenotyping of SDoH and psychosocial factors throughout childhood and adolescence. In addition, in order to examine potential mechanisms by which SDoH during childhood may affect young adult CVH, we obtained measures of epigenetic changes in DNA methylation, and collected 1‐time stool specimens for analysis of the gut microbiome.

### Key Questions

The FF‐CHAYA study, an ancillary study of the core FFCWS study, is funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, with support from Princeton University and Northwestern University. The overarching goal of the FF‐CHAYA study is to understand the role of early‐life social and structural exposures through childhood in the evolution of young adult CVH and CVD, and potential mediation by epigenetic changes. FFCWS collected detailed data on offspring and their environments at birth and at ages 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, and 22 years, with samples for epigenetic (genome‐wide DNA methylation), genotype, and telomere length measurements collected at years 9 and 15. A particular strength of FFCWS is the wealth of data on both parents (including maternal genotype and DNA methylation) and many facets of respondents’ family, neighborhood, school, and behavioral lives since birth. Thus, FF‐CHAYA is designed as a longitudinal study that addresses the following specific questions:

- Are early‐life SDoH associated with CVH in young adulthood? If so, which SDoH are associated with CVH and with which aspects of CVH? Do associations differ by self‐identified sex or race or ethnicity, ancestry, socioeconomic status, or trajectories of social adversity during childhood?

- Are early‐life SDoH associated with early evidence of arterial injury, as determined by carotid ultrasound measures, in young adulthood? Do associations differ by self‐identified sex or race or ethnicity, ancestry, socioeconomic status, or trajectories of social adversity during childhood?

- Do epigenetic DNA methylation profiles mediate some longitudinal associations between upstream, early‐life SDoH exposures and downstream young adult CVH and arterial injury measures? Do underlying genetic effects modify associations of DNA methylation with CVH and arterial injury?

## METHODS

### Core Study Cohort

The FF‐CHAYA study sample described herein is a subcohort of the longstanding FFCWS. 47 FFCWS enrolled a birth cohort of nearly 5000 children and mother dyads at the time of birth in 20 large US cities (population >200 000) between 1998 and 2000, with oversampling of babies born to unmarried parents. As a result, the FFCWS core cohort comprises a large number of ethnic and racial minority groups, immigrants, and low‐income families, with a high prevalence of severe adversity and stressful experiences. For example, at baseline, more than one third of FFCWS mothers had less than a high school degree, and more than one third of families lived below the poverty line. Almost half of mothers identified as non‐Hispanic Black and more than one quarter as Hispanic. There have been 7 waves of data collection occurring at birth (age 0) and approximate ages 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, and 22 years of the offspring. Most data have been collected through interviewer‐ and self‐administered questionnaires focused on social phenotyping, education, and family structure, with additional data collection related to adverse environmental exposures. Both the FFCWS and the FF‐CHAYA study are approved by the Institutional Review Board at Princeton University (which has reliance agreements with all involved centers), and all participants of both studies have provided written informed consent for all study procedures. All data are available on reasonable request from the Coordinating Center of FFCWS. Some deidentified data are freely available on the FFCWS website (https://ffcws.princeton.edu/).

### SDoH Data Available in FFCWS

A particular strength of FFCWS is the wealth of longitudinal data on many facets of participants’ family, neighborhood, school, and behavioral exposures since birth (Table S1, 47 ). FFCWS contains rich information pertaining to both the physical and social environments of the children at infancy through childhood and adolescence. SDoH variables collected to date include conventional measures of socioeconomic position at different stages of the youth, such as schooling and education (throughout childhood and young adulthood, and in parents), parental income and debts/assets, poverty status, and employment (young adult and parents). SDoH measures in FFCWS also comprise measures of childhood adversity at the parental, family, and household level, such as child abuse and neglect, parental violence, parental incarceration, father absence, maternal depression, parental substance use, unstable family structure, household disorder, poor housing quality, lack of health insurance and weak social support, as well as positive exposures such as constructive engagement of father, strong relationship with mother, family stability, and social support from family and friends. SDoH determinants at the neighborhood and community level comprise parental and interviewer reports, and measures linked to external aggregates, including neighborhood violence and disorder, social cohesion and social control, air pollution levels, economic deprivation (eg, % receiving public assistance, % below poverty level, % unemployed, % vacant housing), % with higher education, and racial composition. Researchers have developed complex measures that capture multiple components of adverse childhood experiences. 49 , 50 , 51 Physiological measures of health and detailed data on diet and exercise had not been collected to date in the FFCWS participants.

### Recruitment of the FF‐CHAYA Sample

Recruitment to the FF‐CHAYA sample was managed by Westat, Inc., a clinical research contracting organization that has managed FFCWS participant contact, recruitment, and retention for several waves of data collection. FFCWS allowed recruitment into the FF‐CHAYA ancillary study only after a participant had completed the year 22 data collection for FFCWS. At the year 22 data collection, participants were asked if they would agree to be contacted for a study of heart health. For those who agreed, within several months of completion of the year 22 wave of data collection by FFCWS in each targeted city, 2 Westat recruiters contacted offspring participants who had completed their year 22 data collection and lived within an appropriate distance to travel to a planned in‐person clinic to receive a FF‐CHAYA study in‐person examination. Initially, 2 separate clinics were planned in each of 12 original FFCWS cities. However, contact with offspring participants indicated that they currently live in several metropolitan areas across the United States that were not original FFCWS cities. Therefore, plans were revised over the course of the study to perform in‐person examinations in additional cities and to revisit cities with larger numbers of remaining unexamined participants after the first clinic.

Recruitment efforts were affected by several factors, including incentive amounts and clinic recruitment timelines. To strengthen recruitment, incentives were offered to participants who completed the exam and CA ultrasonography and who traveled longer distances to the clinic. Throughout the study, clinic incentives were expanded and increased. Additionally, significant challenges from COVID‐19 continued through much of the first year of study implementation. Many initial clinics were scheduled during COVID‐19 restrictions for in‐person gatherings. Indeed, 3 early clinics were canceled due to high incidences of COVID‐19 in those cities.

As the COVID‐19 pandemic evolved and participants returned to more usual work or school schedules, we adjusted incentives and travel stipends (with approval from the Princeton Institutional Review Board) based on feedback from attending and nonattending participants. Specifically, after October 2021, we increased the participant incentives from $100 to $200 for completing the visit, and we increased travel stipends over the course of the study, providing a more responsive matrix that varied in a graded fashion depending on the distance traveled to the clinic site, from $25 for participants who traveled 0 to 19 miles to $100 for those traveling >125 miles. We also provided personalized travel support to many participants, by providing step‐by‐step driving or transportation directions, or paying for and arranging ride‐share services. Childcare stipends were also added to assist participants who required babysitting for their young children, in response to participant feedback. As reported elsewhere, the increase in participant incentives, the increase in travel stipends, and the additional travel support were each significantly associated in multivariable analysis with greater likelihood of scheduling an appointment and attending an examination. Greater distance from the participant's home to the clinic site was associated inversely with attendance at the in‐person examination. 52

### Conduct of the In‐Person Examinations

Overall, 33 in‐person examination sessions were conducted in 22 metropolitan areas from September 2021 to September 2023 (Table 1). Three planned clinics (one in August 2021 and 2 in January 2022) among the first 8 were canceled and rescheduled at the discretion of the investigators owing to high activity of the COVID‐19 in those cities at the time. Pop‐up clinics, typically located in hotel ballrooms, occurred over 2 to 3 days depending on the number of participants scheduled; the mean number of participants examined per clinic was 43.1±20.2, the median (interquartile range) was 34 (31–49) and the overall number seen per clinic ranged from 16 to 91 participants, with a total of 1421 young adults participating across clinics. The mean duration of the study visit for participants was approximately 2 hours.

Pop‐up clinics occurred approximately every 3 weeks. All required materials (eg, blood sample tubes, scales) and equipment (eg, centrifuges, blood pressure devices) for each pop‐up clinic were shipped to the site by ExamOne (a contract research organization; Quest Diagnostics) several days before the start of each examination.

After participants checked in at the clinic with Westat personnel, each was escorted to a private examination area. All questions were answered and written informed consent was obtained by the study coordinator after participants watched a 5‐minute video explaining the nature and potential risks of the study. Participants underwent blood pressure measurement and anthropometry measurement, after which phlebotomy was performed. Participant tracking and data entry by technicians were performed in real time using Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) software, which was housed at the Department of Preventive Medicine at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and accessed via a secured VPN portal. Participants were then provided with an iPad tablet and asked to perform the self‐administered questionnaires in REDCap. Technicians were available to assist participants with comprehension of questions during this phase but were instructed not to assist with or direct answers. Participants were then escorted to the carotid ultrasound scanning booth, where they underwent blood pressure measurement and carotid ultrasound scanning. Finally, participants had an exit interview with the study coordinator and were offered the opportunity to participate in an ancillary study of home‐based stool collection for assessment of the microbiome.

### Blood Pressure Measurement

Measurements were obtained by trained ExamOne technicians using a standardized protocol that was modeled after blood pressure measurement techniques used in the CARDIA (Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults) study. 53 Cuff size was determined with the participant standing and measurement of the right arm circumference was taken at the midpoint between the acromion and the olecranon. The participant was then seated comfortably with both feet on the floor, back and arm supported, and the cuff was applied to the right arm. The participant was left alone to sit quietly for 5 minutes before blood pressure measurement. Three serial blood pressure measurements were then obtained using the Omron HEM907XL device with 30 seconds between each measurement. The average of the second and third measures for systolic and diastolic blood pressure was used.

### Anthropometry

Measurements were obtained by trained ExamOne technicians using a standardized protocol that was modeled after anthropometry techniques used in the CARDIA study. 54 Height was measured using a standardized stadiometer and measurements were rounded to the nearest half centimeter. Weight was measured using electronic scales with participants wearing only light clothing, and measurements were rounded down to the nearest 0.5 pounds. Waist girth was measured twice (rounded to the nearest half centimeter) using standardized measuring tapes applied horizontally at a level midway between the iliac crest and the lowest lateral portion of the rib cage; results of the 2 measurements were averaged. Hip girth was also measured twice (rounded to the nearest half centimeter) at the level of the symphysis pubis anteriorly and posteriorly at the level of the maximal protrusion of the gluteal muscles; results of the 2 measurements were averaged. BMI was calculated as the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters.

### Blood‐Based Laboratory Measures

Phlebotomy was performed by ExamOne technicians from the antecubital vein of participants at the in‐person examination in the nonfasting state. A total of ~50 mL of whole blood was obtained, including 2 10 mL serum (red top) tubes; 1 2 mL K2 EDTA (pink top) tube; 1 4 mL, 1 6 mL, and 1 10 mL K2 EDTA (purple top) tube; 1 2.5 mL PAXgene Blood DNA Tube (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ); and 1 2.5 mL PAXgene RNA Tube (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ). Serum tubes were stored at room temperature for 60 to 90 minutes before centrifuging. EDTA tubes were stored on ice for <15 minutes before processing (as needed). The pink top EDTA tube was kept refrigerated until shipping. The 4 mL purple top EDTA tube was maintained at room temperature and prepared for transfer to a Quest Diagnostics laboratory for measurement of a complete blood count and differential. The remaining EDTA and serum tubes were centrifuged per protocol and samples were then transferred to storage tubes. PAXgene tubes were maintained at room temperature before shipping to the Notterman laboratory at Princeton University.

Plasma, serum and packed red blood cell storage tubes were shipped with ice packs overnight to the Laboratory for Clinical Biochemistry Research at the University of Vermont. The following assays were performed, and remaining samples were aliquoted and frozen for long‐term storage: (1) a lipid panel (total cholesterol, high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides, and calculated low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol); (2) a 17‐component metabolic panel (including electrolytes, transaminases, creatinine); (3) hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c); (4) hs‐CRP (high‐sensitivity C‐reactive protein); and (5) SARS‐CoV‐2 serologies. The lipid panel, metabolic panel, and HbA1c assays were performed at the University of Vermont Medical Center and select results were reported to participants. The remaining assays were performed at the Laboratory for Clinical Biochemistry Research. Chemistry assays (lipids, metabolic panel) were performed using the Ortho Vitros 5600 platform (QuidelOrtho Corporation, San Diego, CA), a well‐established clinical laboratory platform. HbA1c was assayed by capillary electrophoresis on the Sebia Capillarys 3 Tera platform (Sebia Inc., Norcross, GA). hs‐CRP was assayed on the Siemens BN‐II platform (Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc., Malvern, PA). The MSD V‐Plex COVID‐19 Coronavirus Panel 2 (IgG) kit (MESO Scale Diagnostics, LLC, Rockville, MD) was used to measure SARS‐CoV‐2 spike (S1), nucleocapsid, and receptor‐binding domain antigen. All coefficients of variation were <10%, most were <5%, and a few were <1% (eg, hs‐CRP). The University of Vermont Medical Center laboratories are both Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments and New York State certified and participate in all relevant College of American Pathologists proficiency surveys (eg, the College of American Pathologists General Chemistry and Therapeutic Drugs Survey C1), as well as the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program and College of American Pathologists HbA1c proficiency survey. All runs contained appropriate control materials for online and longer‐term quality assessment and quality control.

### Self‐Administered Questionnaires

Participants answered standardized questions on an iPad tablet using REDCap survey mode. Five consecutive questionnaires (covering medical history, dietary screener, physical activity, tobacco use, and alcohol use) were administered with total time for participants averaging approximately 20 minutes for this portion of the exam. In the medical history questionnaire, participants were asked to rate their overall health and then were asked a series of health history questions modeled after the NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey) medical history questionnaire. 55 Specifically, participants were asked “Has a doctor or nurse ever said that you have …” with a sequential list of 20 acute and chronic mental and physical health conditions and diagnoses. Any “yes” answer prompted further questions about specific diagnoses and age at diagnosis. Participants were also asked about current medications, reproductive history, weight history, and COVID‐19 history and symptoms. The latter questions were selected to harmonize with the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute C4R (Cross‐Cohort Collaboration). 56 Dietary intake information was collected using the Dietary Screener Questionnaire from NHANES 2009 to 2010. 57 The Dietary Screener Questionnaire is a 26‐item screener that asks about the frequency of consumption of selected foods and beverages in the past month. The Dietary Screener Questionnaire captures intakes of fruits and vegetables, dairy, calcium, added sugars, whole grains, fibers, red meat, and processed meat. Quantitative estimates for intakes of each of the food groups and nutrients were calculated using publicly available scoring algorithms derived from NHANES 2009 to 2010 data. Additional questions addressed habits such as eating out and eating fast food. Physical activity was assessed using the Physical Activity Questionnaire version K questionnaire used by NHANES. 58 Participants were asked the frequency and duration of leisure‐time physical activities, such as sports, fitness, and recreational activities at either a vigorous (large increases in breathing or heart rate) or a moderate (small increase in breathing or heart rate) level in a typical week. Tobacco use was assessed using the CARDIA study tobacco use questionnaire, 59 and alcohol use was assessed using the NHANES alcohol use questionnaire. 60

### Cardiovascular Health Metrics and Measures

The original study plan was to assess the 7 metrics of CVH using the American Heart Association Life's Simple 7 scoring algorithm, 61 which included the 7 metrics of diet, physical activity, smoking exposure, BMI, total blood cholesterol, blood glucose, and blood pressure. During the conduct of the FF‐CHAYA study, the American Heart Association updated and enhanced the metrics and scoring of CVH and introduced Life's Essential 8 (LE8), 62 including the addition of a new metric of sleep duration. Sleep duration is available from the FFCWS core examination surveys at year 22, so this was incorporated for sleep duration measurement in FF‐CHAYA participants. In addition, questions regarding sleep duration were added for the FF‐CHAYA survey‐only participants. Life's Simple 7 cardiovascular health scores (0–2 points for each metric, summed to provide an overall Life's Simple 7 score of 0–14 points [higher is better CVH]) and LE8 scores (0–100 points for each metric, averaged to provide an overall LE8 score of 0–100 points [higher is better CVH]) were calculated to assess individual CVH metrics and overall CVH as recommended by the American Heart Association. 62 Individual CVH metrics were assessed as follows (Table S2).

#### Diet (Available for All [In‐Person and Survey‐Only] Participants)

To calculate the diet score, particular focus was given to 6 components: adequate intakes of fruits and vegetables, fiber, whole grains, dairy, and calcium and limited intake of sugar‐sweetened beverages. The intake of each component was ranked (scale 0–100) separately and the average was computed as the Dietary Screener Questionnaire diet score. These data were then quintiled to generate LE8 scores.

#### Physical Activity (All Participants)

Data on minutes per week of reported moderate and vigorous physical activity were used to calculate LE8 scores. One minute of vigorous‐intensity activity is about the same as 2 minutes of moderate‐intensity activity, so scoring was performed accordingly.

#### Sleep (All Participants)

Average hours of sleep per night were used to assess sleep duration and to generate LE8 scores. Sleep data were not collected in the FF‐CHAYA in‐person examination. From the core FFCWS questionnaires we used the year 22 sleep pattern data on bedtime and work schedules to estimate the sleep duration. The respondents were asked, “Time goes to bed on work or school nights on work or school days/nonwork or school days?” and “Time usually wake up on work or school days/nonwork or school days?” We computed the sleep duration on school days and nonschool days separately using the interval of their reported bedtime and wake time. The average sleep duration was calculated as (school/work sleep duration×5+nonschool/work duration×2)/7. If the participant only had 1 of workday and nonworkday sleep duration computed, then it was taken as the final sleep duration.

#### Nicotine Exposure (All Participants)

Use of combustible tobacco products as well as exposure to nicotine‐containing e‐cigarettes or vaping products, and secondhand smoke exposure, were assessed to generate the LE8 score. Smoking status was determined based on responses to questionnaires regarding the use of cigarettes over the past 30 days, and the recent usage of e‐cigarette and other tobacco in the past week. Hours of secondhand exposure in the household was collected to evaluate exposure to secondhand smoke.

#### Body‐Mass Index (All Participants)

Directly measured height and weight were used to calculate BMI (as weight in kg divided by the square of the height in meters) for in‐person examination participants. For survey‐only participants, self‐reported height and weight were used to calculate BMI. These respective BMI values were then used to generate LE8 scores for each group for this metric.

#### Blood Lipids (In‐Person Participants)

Nonhigh‐density lipoprotein cholesterol cholesterol levels were used to generate LE8 scores. Medication usage was assessed on the self‐administered REDCap medical history questionnaire.

#### Blood Pressure (In‐Person Participants)

Average systolic and diastolic blood pressure measures were used to generate the LE8 score. Antihypertensive medication usage was assessed on the self‐administered REDCap medical history questionnaire.

#### Glycemia (In‐Person Participants)

Given that participants were nonfasting at the time of phlebotomy, we used the HbA1c measures to calculate LE8 scores. Self‐reported diabetes was assessed on the self‐administered REDCap medical history questionnaire.

### Carotid Ultrasonography

All carotid ultrasound scans were performed by 1 of 2 highly experienced sonographers from the University of Wisconsin‐Madison Atherosclerosis Imaging Research Program core ultrasound center, who traveled to each of the in‐person examinations. With participants resting supine, transverse and longitudinal images from the clavicle to the most superior portion of the internal CA were acquired on the right and left side, each from 2 angles of insonation using a Mindray M9 ultrasound system and an L12‐4s linear array ultrasound transducer (Mahwah, NJ, USA). Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine images were imported into Siemens Syngo Ultrasound Work Place reading stations (Mountain View, CA) at the University of Wisconsin‐Madison Atherosclerosis core laboratory. Siemens Arterial Health Package software was used to measure end‐diastolic mean and maximum intima‐media thickness of the distal 1.0 cm of the far walls of the right and left common CAs (CCAs), the proximal 1.0 cm of the far walls of the right and left CA bifurcation segments, and the proximal 1.0 cm of the right and left internal CA, each in triplicate. 34 , 63 , 64 The primary carotid IMT outcome measures were mean CCA IMT (the mean of all mean IMT measures from the right and left CCA segments) and max composite IMT (mean of all maximum IMT measures from the CCA, bifurcation, and internal CA segments). The number of CA plaques in each of the 12 segments visualized was summed to create a plaque score.

Systolic and diastolic CA diameters were measured in triplicate using a digital edge tracing tool and from 2 to 3 consecutive cardiac cycles using Access Point Web version 3.0 (Freeland Systems, LLC, Westminster, CO). 64 , 65 , 66 Standardized measurement of oscillometric brachial artery blood pressures were obtained simultaneously to permit accurate calculation of the CA distensibility coefficient and Young's elastic modulus.

Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine files containing images of the distal CCAs at end‐diastole were converted to bitmap images for grayscale analysis using LifeQ Medical Carotid Plaque Texture Analysis Software V4.8 (Nicosia, Cyprus). Grayscale echogenicity and texture features analyzed for this study included grayscale median, entropy, contrast, and angular second moment. Images were normalized and standardized to a pixel density of 20 pix/mm. 46 , 67 , 68 The far wall of the distal CCA was segmented by tracing the blood‐intima interface and media adventitia interface for a distance of 1.0 cm and grayscale texture features were extracted. The primary CA echogenicity outcome measure was grayscale median.

The University of Wisconsin‐Madison Atherosclerosis is the core ultrasound reading center for several large epidemiological studies. In all studies, reproducibility was excellent as it was in this study. In FF‐CHAYA, carotid IMT scans were measured by 2 readers. The intraclass correlation coefficient for intrareader reproducibility for mean CCA IMT was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.98–0.99) for reader 1 and 0.99 (95% CI, 0.97–0.99) for reader 2. The intraclass correlation coefficient for interreader mean CCA IMT was 0.98 (95% CI, 0.96–0.99). A single reader performed all CA distensibility measurements; their intraclass correlation coefficient for distensibility coefficient was 0.93 (95% CI, 0.85–0.97) and for Young's elastic modulus it was 0.90 (95% CI, 0.77–0.96). A single reader performed all grayscale median measurements; their intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.99–0.99).

Mean–mean carotid IMT (mm) was calculated as the mean of the right and left mean IMT of 3 measured R waves from an anterior approach and thr3ee from a posterior approach of the distal 1 cm of the CCA far walls. Mean–maximum IMT (mm) was calculated by the mean of the right and left mean of the maximum IMT of 3 measured R waves from an anterior approach and 3 from a posterior approach of the distal 1 cm of the CCA far walls, bulbs, and proximal 1 cm of the internal CAs. IMT values are measures of subclinical arterial injury. Grayscale median was calculated from the mean of the right and left average of 2 tracings from the distal 1 cm of the far wall of the CCAs, with lower values representing plaques that are more lipid‐rich and representative of higher cardiovascular risk. 69 Distensibility coefficient (mm Hg‐1) was calculated by (end‐systolic diameter 2− end‐diastolic diameter 2)/(pulse pressure* end‐diastolic diameter 2). Young's elastic modulus (mm Hg) was calculated by (end‐diastolic diameter /wall thickness)/distensibility coefficient. These are measurements of arterial stiffness.

### DNA Collection and Storage

Saliva DNA collection for epigenetic analyses was performed during the core FFCWS study year 22 examination and repeated during the in‐person FF‐CHAYA examination for attending participants. In addition, blood was collected from FF‐CHAYA in‐person participants for DNA isolation. After onsite processing by ExamOne technicians, saliva and blood samples were shipped from clinic exam sites to the Notterman laboratory at Princeton University for processing and storage of DNA.

Saliva was collected using the OGR Discover OGR600 saliva collection kit (DNA Genotek, Ottawa, ON, Canada). Participants were instructed on optimal technique to generate saliva and fill the tube to the fill line. The funnel was removed and the tube was capped securely and shaken a minimum of 5 times. Samples were then placed in biohazard bags for shipping. DNA from saliva was extracted using the prep•ITL2P reagent according to the manufacturer's instructions. Following extraction, saliva DNA was quantified, aliquoted, and stored at −80 °C.

Blood samples were collected in Paxgene tubes for isolation of DNA or RNA from peripheral blood mononuclear cells, the pellets shipped on dry ice to the Notterman laboratory, arriving within 24 hours of phlebotomy. DNA extraction was performed using the DNeasy and Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Germantown) and DNA quantity and quality were assessed by measurement of A260, A280, and A230 before storage at −80 °C. RNA was processed with the RNAeasy Kit (Qiagen, Germantown) and quantity and quality were similarly assessed before storage at −80 °C. To account for variability in leukocyte counts and composition, an aliquot of EDTA‐collected blood was processed by Quest Diagnostics to obtain a complete blood count with differential count on the day of phlebotomy. Epigenetic analysis of whole‐genome DNA methylation is being performed using the Infinium Methylation EPIC v2.0 (Illumina, San Diego, CA). at the University of Chicago Genomic Facility.

### Conduct of the Survey‐Only Data Collection

For participants who lived too far from a clinic or did not schedule appointments, or who scheduled an appointment but did not attend a clinic, we offered the opportunity to participate in the electronic survey only after all in‐person examinations were completed. Contacts were made via regular mail in week 1, followed by email or text in weeks 2 through 6 (based on participant contact preferences), and finally by FedEx thereafter as the survey continued if the participant did not respond to prior attempts. Survey‐only participants received the same 5 questionnaires as in‐person participants, with the addition of questions regarding sleep duration, as noted previously. Participants entered responses on secure REDCap forms managed at Northwestern University. The survey‐only portion was undertaken from September to December 2023.

### Statistical Analysis

All statistical analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS institute Inc, Cary, NC). For FF‐CHAYA participants, unweighted mean±SD were reported for continuous variables and frequencies (percentages) were reported for categorical variables. Characteristics were compared across cohort data of core, in‐person, and survey‐only participants using Welch's ANOVA for continuous variables and the chi‐square tests for categorical variables with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons when indicated. A 2‐sided P<0.05 was considered statistically significant. Detailed methods for applying the LE8 scoring algorithm for each of the metrics to FF‐CHAYA are provided in Table S2. To contextualize the cardiovascular health of FF‐CHAYA participants relative to a nationally representative sample, we compared our cohort's LE8 scores with those of US young adults aged 20 to 25 years from NHANES. SAS procedures SURVEYFREQ and SURVEYMEANS were used to incorporate the complex multistage sampling design of NHANES in the statistical analysis. To create a larger sample, data from 3 2‐year cycles of the continuous NHANES were combined for 2015 through March 2020. Per NHANES analytical guidelines for combining data across cycles, sample weights were constructed with rescaling of the weights such that the sum of weights matched the survey population at the midpoint of each survey period. LE8 score calculation in NHANES data was performed as described previously. 70

The investigators initially projected that a sample size of 2400 participants would attend the in‐person examination, with 1800 of these participants undergoing carotid ultrasound measurements. As noted, there were some difficulties with recruitment owing to infection safety issues and societal disruptions associated with the COVID‐19 pandemic. With an expected sample size of 2400 participants, we calculated that we would have >90% power (at an alpha of 0.05) to detect clinically meaningful differences in continuous measures, such as the 14‐point Life's Simple 7 score or 100‐point LE8 score, and in component measures such as blood pressure or cholesterol, across 2 groups (eg, those exposed/unexposed to a given SDoH), and across a wide range of sample sizes and effect sizes. We also calculated >80% power to detect meaningful differences in proportions (≥5% absolute differences between groups) across a wide range of sample sizes and proportions. For carotid ultrasound measurements, we assumed a mean maximal carotid IMT of 0.65 mm (±0.10 mm), providing >90% power with 1800 participants and >80% power with 1440 participants to detect a difference of ≥0.03 mm between 2 groups (a difference that has been associated with clinical CVD outcomes in older adults) across a wide range of sample sizes per group.

The investigators had full access to all data and the funder had no role in decisions regarding analyses or publications. Dr Lloyd‐Jones and Dr Ning had full access to all of the data for the current analyses and they take responsibility for their integrity and the data analysis.

## RESULTS

### FF‐CHAYA Study Sample

A total of 2507 young adults from the core FFCWS cohort were eligible and invited to participate in the FF‐CHAYA clinics (Figure). Among these, 1857 scheduled a clinic appointment and 1421 attended a clinic for an in‐person examination. Overall clinic participation rate was 76.5% of those who scheduled an appointment and 56.7% of those eligible. Of the 1421 young adults examined in person over the course of the FF‐CHAYA study, data are presented here for 1375 participants, after excluding participants with key missing data (N=13) and participants who were pregnant at the time of the examination (N=33; excluded for the present analysis given the substantial changes in all LE8 metrics that may occur at varying points during gestation). An additional 620 young adults (44.9% of 1381 participants who were offered the opportunity) responded electronically to the survey‐only portion of the FF‐CHAYA examination. Data are presented for 600 participants after excluding 3 with key missing data and 17 who were currently pregnant. In total, 2041 FF‐CHAYA participants provided data through either the in‐person examination or the survey, representing 81.4% of eligible young adults.

The mean LE8 score for FF‐CHAYA participants who attended the in‐person examination was in the moderate CVH range at 69.2±13.0 points (out of 100; Tables 2 and 3). For the 5 metrics common to the in‐person and survey‐only participants (ie diet., physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep, and BMI) mean CVH score was 59.2±18.4 points (out of 100). Among the individual LE8 component metrics, diet and physical activity score means were in the low range (<50 points), BMI and nicotine exposure scores were in the moderate range (50–79 points), and sleep, lipid, blood pressure, and blood glucose scores were in the high range (80–100 points).

Among the entire FF‐CHAYA cohort, male and female participants had similar overall LE8 scores and LE8 health behavior scores, although male participants had somewhat higher (better) physical activity and BMI scores, whereas women had slightly higher (better) nicotine exposure scores (Table 2). When stratified by race and ethnicity (Table 3), White participants had the highest and Black participants the lowest overall LE8 and LE8 health behavior scores, with the largest absolute differences in the physical activity and BMI metrics.

### Comparison of FF‐CHAYA Samples With Core FFCWS Cohort

Characteristics of early‐life SDoH in the FF‐CHAYA in‐person participants and survey‐only participants are presented separately in Table 5, along with characteristics of the core FFCWS cohort (from which FF‐CHAYA participants were recruited) for comparison. Overall, the FF‐CHAYA samples were similar to, and representative of, the core FFCWS cohort. The mean age of in‐person FF‐CHAYA attendees was 22.9 years, and of survey‐only participants was 24.0 years. Each of these was significantly older than the core cohort, as expected given the sequential nature of the data collection periods. Both the in‐person and survey FF‐CHAYA samples had modestly but statistically significantly lower proportions of male participants compared with the core cohort. Characteristics of the core FFCWS, FF‐CHAYA in‐person, and FF‐CHAYA survey cohorts were otherwise similar overall, with several exceptions. At birth, survey‐only participants' mothers tended to have somewhat higher income (as reflected by % of federal poverty level) compared with the other 2 groups, and fathers' incomes at birth tended to be somewhat higher for survey versus in‐person FF‐CHAYA participants. Regarding absolute values of health factors that comprise the LE8 score (Table 6), core FFCWS participants were somewhat more likely to be current smokers and to self‐report a lower BMI level. Prevalences of treatment for hypertension and self‐reported diagnosis of diabetes were significantly lower in the overall core cohort compared with the FF‐CHAYA samples, although these conditions were uncommon (occurring in <2% of participants) and differences across the 3 cohort samples were small (≤1% absolute difference in prevalence).

## DISCUSSION

The FF‐CHAYA study leverages an existing, longitudinal, high‐quality social science study, traditional and novel measures of health, and state‐of‐the art imaging to help advance our understanding of whether, to what extent, and how early‐life social determinants may affect young adult CVH and early arterial injury. It also enhances investigation of potential mechanisms whereby external SDoH in childhood may “get under the skin” to affect lifelong health outcomes. Several features of the study design and data merit consideration, with implications for both public health and precision medicine strategies.

### Innovative Features

The limitations of previous studies of early‐life SDoH and their associations with adult health outcomes are well described. Many studies of children have collected high‐quality data on SDoH but have not followed participants into adulthood for health outcomes. More commonly, investigators have asked young adults to report measures of childhood SDoH retrospectively, with high potential for recall bias, misclassification, and type 1 and type 2 errors. To start a contemporary study of SDoH from the beginning of life and wait for adult health outcomes in the same individuals is generally not feasible.

The FF‐CHAYA study catalyzes the investigation of childhood SDoH‐young adult health associations through several innovative features. First, embedding the health phenotyping of young adults within an existing study started at birth provides remarkable efficiency with regard to timing (no need to wait decades for health measures) and recruitment and study infrastructure (participants already engaged with the ongoing core study). Second, the innovative use of “pop‐up” clinics minimized overhead and participant travel costs that would have been associated with fixed site clinics and allowed the opportunity for investigators to meet participants “where they are” in >20 cities across the country. Third, the use of the CVH construct as an outcome provides relevant insight into the current health status of the young adults, while also serving as an ideal intermediate surrogate end point measure that is known to be strongly associated with both upstream SDoH exposures and downstream clinical outcomes that typically occur decades later. Fourth, the availability of state‐of the‐art, noninvasive imaging of the CA allows for detection of early arterial injury at a time of life when frank atherosclerosis is rare, yet vascular damage is already beginning. Finally, the availability of repeated, detailed SDoH measurement at the level of individual, family, and neighborhood across 7 waves of data collection from birth to age 22 years, and DNA collection (ages 9, 15, and 22 years) in the core FFCWS study, as well as DNA/RNA collection in the FF‐CHAYA cohort, will promote insight into the complex interactions and temporal sequencing of environmental, genetic, and epigenetic influences on health in younger life. Thus, the FF‐CHAYA study represents a unique opportunity to study early‐life origins of complex adult phenotypes in the longest‐running contemporary birth cohort of young adults from across the United States.

### Recruitment and Study Conduct

The experience of the FF‐CHAYA study provides insights into cohort recruitment and retention of young adults, largely from disadvantaged backgrounds, in the contemporary environment and amid the challenges of the COVID‐19 pandemic. Careful assessment of successful recruitment strategies in real time by the recruitment team allowed for enhanced location, contact, follow‐up, and support of participants by the recruitment team. Adjustments to the recruitment team staffing allowed for on‐the‐ground recruitment (including enhanced participant finding and actual door‐knocking). In addition, based on participant feedback regarding challenges of attending in‐person examinations, changes and additions were made to enhance incentive amounts, travel stipends, travel logistics support, and childcare stipends. These adjustments proved invaluable to the success of recruitment.

### Findings and Cohort Characteristics

The FF‐CHAYA cohort, as represented by the in‐person and survey‐only samples, is representative of both the FFCWS core study, from which it is drawn, and US young adults more broadly, especially those from disadvantaged social backgrounds. Over half of the FF‐CHAYA sample identified as female, nearly half as Black, and another quarter as Hispanic, providing key insights into groups often underrepresented in clinical and population‐based research.

Overall quantitative CVH scores were suboptimal in FF‐CHAYA participants, falling in the moderate range. Diet and physical activity scores were especially poor, and the most notable finding was a mean BMI of 29.0 in this young adult cohort. Whereas mean levels of blood pressure, glycemia, and lipids were within clinically normal ranges, the high prevalence of overweight and obesity likely portend earlier onset and greater cumulative exposure to adverse levels of these risk factors, with concomitantly accelerated cardiovascular damage and earlier clinical events. Indeed, the findings from the carotid ultrasonography in these young adults with a mean age of 23 years appear ominous, with mean carotid IMT levels on par with approximately 33‐year‐old average healthy adults in the general population. 71 , 72 Among middle‐aged and older adults, greater carotid IMT is consistently associated with higher risk for incident CVD, CHD, and especially stroke. 73 In an individual‐level meta‐analysis of cohorts with mean ages of 50 to 70 years old, each 0.1 mm higher mean common carotid IMT (slightly higher than the SD observed in our study) was associated with 9% greater risk for CVD. 44

### Ongoing and Future Work

Ongoing analyses and future reports will address the key questions noted, including associations of SDoH and LE8 with carotid measures, and potential mechanisms. Characterization of longitudinal SDoH exposures is complex, especially in childhood, and associations with CVH and carotid outcomes may be unpredictable. DNA methylation from both saliva (at years 9 and 15 in FFCWS participants) and whole blood leukocytes (from year 22 FF‐CHAYA participants) has been fully assayed and analyses examining associations with upstream SDoH, downstream CVH, and carotid analyses are ongoing. Once these associations are established, formal mediation and causal inference analyses can be undertaken to understand whether epigenetic DNA methylation may serve as a mediator of associations between childhood SDoH and health outcomes. Many further analyses are planned to examine specific SDoH exposures and specific CVH outcomes, including individual CVH metrics and carotid measures. A biorepository of saliva and blood specimens has been established at Princeton University, and ongoing work is assaying a broad array of proteomic markers of inflammation, as well as data from the gut microbiome ancillary study. Future plans also include a focus on lipidomics in the FF‐CHAYA participants. A second examination cycle for FF‐CHAYA participants is being planned in conjunction with future waves of FFCWS engagement.

### Implications for SDoH Research

The loss of CVH from birth to midlife has been well described in many populations. However, it is unknown which SDoH may be most important and whether there are critical periods of exposure that drive loss of CVH. In addition, the biological mechanisms by which SDoH may drive loss of CVH from birth to young adulthood remain to be clarified. Recently, epigenetic mechanisms have been implicated as potential mediators of the link between environmental exposures and health. 22 , 74 , 75 Data from the CARDIA study have shown significant associations between trajectories of CVH across young adulthood with epigenetic age acceleration measures and individual CpG methylation sites/methylation quantitative trait loci. 76 , 77 , 78 It is important to extend these observations to early life and understand the temporal associations and all of the implicated biological pathways that may connect childhood adversity with young adult CVH and CVD. The rich and well‐textured repository of social/environmental phenotypes and biological data that this study is developing will uniquely advance these avenues of inquiry.

### Potential Impact on Public Health and Precision Medicine Strategies

CVD remains the leading cause of death and disability for adults in the United States, and, with current trends, the United States will spend >$1.8 trillion annually on care of CVD by 2050. 3 CVD and its risk factors disproportionately affect minoritized and lower socioeconomic status segments of the US population. 1 Data in adults point to a critical role played by early‐life social and environmental factors, particularly for vulnerable populations, in loss of CVH, development of risk factors and subclinical CVD, and ultimately, development of clinical CVD, but such data are retrospective and limited. 79 , 80 The FF‐CHAYA study provides a novel lens through which to examine the prospective effects of social and environmental adversity on CVH from childhood into young adulthood. By examining the key drivers of the loss of CVH, new strategies and areas of focus may be elucidated for community and public health interventions in parents and children. The focus on molecular mechanisms by which social determinants may “get under the skin” to influence health trajectories may also identify new pathways for intervention at the individual patient level to enhance resilience to childhood adversity. Given the burden of cardiometabolic risk factors and CVD in individuals and the population, both of these strategies will likely be needed, to address “sick populations” and “sick individuals,” as suggested by Rose. 81

### Conclusions

The FF‐CHAYA study directly addresses numerous recent calls from governmental and public health organizations to understand and address the social determinants of CVH early in life, promote CVH across the lifespan, and enhance resilience. 13 , 62 , 82 , 83 , 84 , 85 It also will provide unique insights into the potential mechanistic role played by epigenetics in health disparities. Through linkage of social, genetic, physiologic, and preclinical measures we can gain novel perspectives on the social determinants of CVH before early adulthood, and into the potential mechanisms mediating loss of CVH, particularly in vulnerable subgroups that bear a disproportionate burden of CVD. We anticipate identifying critical areas for clinical and population health policies, and potential targets for interventional studies in individuals and groups at risk for loss of CVH.

# Genome-Wide Association Study of Treatment Response to Venlafaxine XR in Generalized Anxiety Disorder

**Authors:** Jeesun Jung; Elisabeth A. Tawa; Christine Muench; Allison D. Rosen; Karl Rickels; Falk W. Lohoff

**Affiliations:** aDivision of Intramural Clinical and Biological Research, National Institute of Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, Bethesda, MD | bSection on Clinical Genomics and Experimental Therapeutics, National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, Bethesda, MD | cDepartment of Psychiatry-Mood and Anxiety Disorders Treatment and Research Program, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA

## Abstract

We conducted the first genome-wide association study (GWAS) in Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) to identify potential predictors of venlafaxine XR treatment outcome. Ninety-eight European Americans (EA) patients participated in a venlafaxine XR clinical trial for GAD, with Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAM-A) response/remission at 24 weeks as the primary outcome measure. All participants were genotyped with the Illumina PsychChip, and 266,820 common single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were analyzed. Although no SNPs reached genome-wide significance, 8 SNPs were marginally associated with treatment response/remission and HAM-A reduction at week 12 and 24 (p < 0.00001). Several identified genes may indicate markers crossing neuropsychiatric diagnostic categories.

## 1. Introduction

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), a chronic psychiatric disorder characterized by a state of excessive worry, afflicts roughly 4.1% of American adults (Grant et al., 2005). GAD is marked by significant morbidity and mortality. Recent studies found that compared to those without anxiety, individuals with GAD had a significantly higher likelihood of suicidal ideation (odds ratios (ORs) = 1.78 – 4.81) and attempted suicides (ORs = 2.70 – 5.59) (Cougle et al., 2009; Kanwar et al., 2013). GAD is most often treated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs). However, antidepressant treatment response is highly variable in individuals with GAD; while antidepressant treatments are effective for some GAD patients, up to 34% of patients fail to respond favorably (Baldwin and Nair, 2005; Gelenberg et al., 2000; Rickels et al., 1993). Pharmacogenetic studies investigating the effect of antidepressant drugs on mood disorders have primarily focused on major depressive disorder (MDD), while research on pharmacogenetic treatments for anxiety disorders is limited (Kato and Serretti, 2010; Multani et al., 2012; Tiwari et al., 2009). Because the research on pharmacogenetic treatment response in anxiety disorders is sparse, the genetic component underlying pharmacotherapy response remains unknown.

To identify genetic variants contributing to the etiology of primary anxiety disorders, a meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWASs) with large, independent samples found multiple novel genetic variants to be significantly associated with anxiety disorder phenotypes (Otowa et al., 2016). GWASs could be useful for examining the pharmacogenetics of antidepressant treatment response in GAD to detect small effect sizes of associated genetic variants.

In this study, we tested the hypothesis that single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are associated with treatment response outcome in GAD. Treatment responses were quantified based on Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAM-A) and Clinical Global Impressions-Severity (CGI) scale reductions following 24-week treatment with venlafaxine XR. Identifying genetic variants which potentially contribute to GAD could better inform pharmacological treatments based on individual genetic profiles.

## 2. Methods

### 2.1 Subjects

Participants with a diagnosis of GAD were enrolled in an 18-month relapse prevention study which included three treatment phases (Rickels et al., 2010): The first phase 24-week open-label venlafaxine XR flexible-dose treatment phase (75–225 mg day−1) was used to conduct primary pharmacogenetic analyses (supplementary materials). Overall, 156 patients (European-Americans [EA] n =112; African-Americans n =41; others n= 3) were evaluated for treatment response to venlafaxine XR. However, due to ethnic differences in allele frequencies and consequent population stratification, only the EA population (n= 112) was used in the pharmacogenetic analysis. The HAM-A score was used as a primary outcome measure, and the CGI of Improvement (CGI-I) score at 24 weeks was used as a secondary outcome measure.

### 2.2 Genotype and Quality Controls

All participants were genotyped using the Illumina PsychChip capturing 571K SNPs. Among those SNPs, only common variants SNPs whose minor allele frequency is greater than 5% were selected due to our sample size. Common variants are defined by over 1% of a minor allele frequency with decent sample size such as 1,000 (Schork et al., 2009), but we selected common SNPs having 5% or greater because at least 5 out of 100 samples were needed for a suitable statistical analysis due to our sample size of 96.

Quality control (QC) procedures were applied to individual samples and SNPs. Using common SNPs (n = 146,257) available in both our samples, and in samples in the 11 populations of HapMap phase 3 data (n = 1,184), we performed principal components analysis to determine non-European ancestry by Eigenstrat (Price et al., 2006). Non-European ancestry samples were removed. Samples were excluded if the missing rate exceeded 2%. Related or duplicated samples were identified through identity-by-state sharing analysis and removed. SNPs were excluded if the missing rate exceeded 5%, their minor allele frequency was < 5%, or they showed departure from the Hardy Weinberg equilibrium test (p-value < 1.0E-5). After the series of QC, 98 European samples with 266,820 common SNPs remained for further statistical analysis (supplementary materials).

### 2.3 Statistical Analysis

The HAM-A reduction scores from baseline to 24 weeks and from baseline to 12 weeks respectively were tested for association with each SNP using a linear regression model based on an additive model. Response and remission to venlafaxine XR at 12 and 24 weeks, including CGI-I response and remission, were tested using an allelic based chi-square test that compared allele frequency between two groups. Instead of using Fisher Exact test that is more accurate than the chi-square test when the sample size is small and a genetic variant is rare, we utilized chi-square test because our sample size of 98 and common variants provide a reasonable approximation of test statistics[reference].

## 3. Results

None of the SNPs were identified with genome-wide significance (1.9×10−7 = 0.05/266,820 by Bonferroni correction based on the number of SNPs, 266,820 SNPs) for either the main outcome measures or secondary outcome measures at the main study end point at week 24. All p-values except HAM-A reduction score were driven by an allelic comparison test without any assumption of genetic model such as a co-dominant model. Additional results are available in the supplementary materials. Table 1 illustrates the 8 SNPs associated with all treatment response/remission measures and HAM-A score at week 24 and 12 by a threshold of p-value < 0.01: rs10483832 (MED6), rs13216187 (SGK1), rs17154827, rs1993919 (STAB2), rs2136474 (SPATA3), rs7060140 (OPHN1), rs7342064 and rs7897283 (PARD3).

## 4. Discussion

In this study, we conducted the first GWAS analysis of antidepressant treatment response in GAD. We found that none of the SNPs tested reached a genome-wide significance threshold, either in categorical outcomes or HAM-A response/remission. We did not explore demographic and clinical characteristics, such as sex, age, and time spent in treatment, as covariates in the association analysis of our sample due to the overall negative result. The following 8 SNPs were marginally associated with treatment response/remission and HAM-A scores at both week 12 and 24 (p < 0.00001): rs10483832-MED6, rs13216187-SGK1, rs17154827, rs1993919-STAB2, rs2136474-SPATA3, rs7060140-OPHN1, rs7342064-PARD3, and rs7897283-PARD3 (Table 1). The finding that these 8 SNPs were consistently associated with treatment outcome across HAM-A measures and time points indicates encouraging trends to pursue for further study.

SGK1 is the most clinically notable of the identified genes. A growing body of literature indicates that SGK1 may be involved in the pathophysiology of mood, anxiety, and trauma-related disorders. Chronic stress exposure in mice has been found to increase SGK1 in corpus callosum oligodendrocytes via hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis activation, inducing morphological changes which may contribute to the pathogenesis of major depressive disorder (Miyata et al., 2015). Furthermore, downregulation of SGK1 in the hippocampus resulted in a reversal of corticosterone-induced depressive symptoms in a rodent model of depression (Li et al., 2015).

Recent studies have also shown that the effect of glucocorticoid signaling on glucocorticoid receptor function may be mediated by SGK1 upregulation, which has been demonstrated in both rodents and humans (Anacker et al., 2011; Sato et al., 2008; Yuen et al., 2011). Traumatic stress has been shown to induce learned helplessness and anhedonic-like behaviors in rats through decreased expression of SGK1 and synaptic significant decrease in spine density in medial prefrontal cortex (PFC) neurons (Licznerski et al., 2015). The same study found the SGK1 gene to be down-regulated by more than 80% in postmortem PFC samples of PTSD individuals compared to healthy controls (Licznerski et al., 2015). Thus these studies support an association between glucocorticoid-induced increases in SGK1 and the development of anxiety and mood disorders. Although a larger sample is needed to replicate the present study’s findings, SGK1 genetic variants may contribute to treatment response and GAD susceptibility.

STAB2 and OPHN1, two additional genes associated with antidepressant treatment outcome in GAD in the present study, have been identified as potential genetic determinants of schizophrenia. An Identify candidate Causal SNPs and Pathways (ICSNPathway) analysis on a schizophrenia GWAS data set implicated STAB2 as a candidate gene in schizophrenia susceptibility. Though OPHN1 has largely been associated with mental retardation (Nakano-Kobayashi et al., 2014), intellectual disability (Powell et al., 2014), and autism spectrum disorders (Piton et al., 2011; Won et al., 2013), reductions in gamma oscillatory activity observed in OPHN1 knockout mice have also been associated with Alzheimer’s disease, aging, and schizophrenia phenotypes, suggesting that reductions in OPHN1 expression increase the likelihood of cognitive and psychiatric pathology (Powell et al., 2014). The common correlations between STAB2 and OPHN1 genetic variants and neuropsychiatric illnesses suggest an underlying genetic basis for the symptomatology shared by these disorders.

Because SGK1, STAB2, and OPHN1 have been associated with a) treatment response in GAD in our study, and b) MDD, PTSD, and schizophrenia across studies, these results suggest that some genetic markers might cross diagnostic categories for multiple psychiatric disorders.

From the standpoints of both genetics and clinical experimental design, the current study may have been limited by several factors, including the retroactive collection of DNA, the absence of a placebo arm in the first phase of the trial, and the use of pill counts as the only measure of medication adherence. It should also be noted that the Illumina PsychChip array is designed on the basis of literature findings, and it contains at least 50,000 markers which have been previously associated with common psychiatric disorders. Hence, it is possible that our method of genotyping increased the probability of identifying genes of prior association with psychiatric disorders.

Limiting factors in the present study were small sample sizes and lack of statistical power for a genome-wide association study. At the same time our phenotypic characteristics were a response/remission to the drug which often drives relatively larger effects by genetic variants than complex disease status does. Considering our study as an exploratory study, the sample size of 98 was suitable enough to provide nominal association signals of SNPs on treatment outcomes of venlafaxine XR due to relatively large effects of SNPs selected from psychiatric disease genetic studies. In addition, instead of using a mixed effective model incorporating different time points for HAM-A score, we took into account HAM-A reduction scores from a baseline of HAM-A to investigate how genetic variants contributed to an improvement of HAM-A scores.

The Illumina Psych Chip that we used for genotyping was customized SNPs selected from results of psychiatric disease GWAS and many Exome studies, therefore SNP markers were not well-covered by common variants. Accurate imputation requires well-covered common variants with strong linkage disequilibrium (LD) across whole genomes (Halperin and Stephan, 2009)(Marchini and Howie, 2010). Due to our customized common SNPs screened by 5% of minor allele frequency with our samples size, the accuracy of imputation was not guaranteed to improve statistical power to discover associations.

In summary, we conducted the first GWAS of antidepressant treatment response in GAD. Although we found no significant genome-wide association results, it is promising that 8 SNPs were marginally associated with treatment response/remission and HAM-A at both months 3 and 6 (p < 0.00001). Because three genes (SGK1, STAB2, and OPHN1) included in our SNPs of interest have been previously associated with mood and anxiety disorders, our results suggest that certain genetic markers may underlie the shared phenotypic characteristics of comorbid psychiatric pathologies. Avenues for future research include the replication of results with larger samples sizes to increase statistical power and further elucidate the treatment effects of antidepressant venlafaxine XR on GAD.
